keyVerseText: And Balaam said unto Balak, Stand by thy burnt offering, and I will go: peradventure the LORD will come to meet me: and whatsoever he sheweth me I will tell thee. And he went to an high place. to an: or, solitary
rootMeaning: The root meaning of שְׁפִי (shᵉphîy) derives from the verb שָׁפָה (shâphâh), which conveys the idea of being high or sticking out, often in the sense of something bare or wind-swept. This root emphasizes a physical prominence or exposed height, such as a bare hill or plain, highlighting not just elevation but also the absence of covering or vegetation. This literal sense enriches the common English gloss of 'high place' by suggesting a stark, exposed vantage point rather than merely any elevated location.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, שְׁפִי consistently refers to elevated, bare places—often locations of significance such as altars or lookout points—appearing in nine instances. The top translations reflect this with phrases like 'to an high place,' 'in high places,' and 'upon all high places,' showing a consistent theme of physical elevation and openness. This uniformity suggests the term is used to denote specific geographical or cultic sites characterized by their exposed, elevated nature.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the concept of שְׁפִי as a bare, high place carries rich symbolism for faith. Such places often serve as settings for divine encounters or worship, emphasizing accessibility and visibility before God. The bareness and height may symbolize spiritual openness and separation from the mundane, inviting believers to a clearer sightline to the divine. Recognizing the original meaning helps Christians appreciate how physical geography in Scripture can reflect spiritual truths about holiness, revelation, and the call to stand exposed yet secure before God.
keyVerseReflection: In Numbers 23:3, Balaam goes 'to an high place' (שְׁפִי), a bare elevated spot where he expects to meet the LORD. The term here highlights the physical and symbolic nature of the location as a place set apart—exposed and prominent—suitable for divine revelation. This usage underscores the importance of such high places as venues where heaven and earth meet, reinforcing the anticipation and solemnity of Balaam's encounter with God.
